name: The State Hermitage Museum
funding: Federal budget of the Russian Federation and state corporate sponsorships (VTB Bank, Gazprom).
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.
highlight: The imperial collection is housed in the Winter Palace.

overview: Art and culture museum in six buildings in Saint Petersburg, including the Winter Palace, the Small, Old and New Hermitage, and the Hermitage Theatre. The General Staff Building and Menshikov Palace have been added (Wikipedia).
Catherine the Great acquired a collection from the Berlin merchant Johann Ernst Gotzkowsky in 1764. The museum marks its founding each year on 7 December (Wikipedia).
It began as the private apartments of the Winter Palace, a residence of the Russian emperors, and is federal state property (Wikipedia).

Mikhail Piotrovsky has directed it since 1992. His father Boris Piotrovsky led it from 1964 to 1990 (Wikipedia). On 10 September 2025 Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin reappointed him for five years (TASS).
A 1996 presidential decree placed the Hermitage under the patronage of the President of the Russian Federation (Decree No. 862 of 12 June 1996).

Visiting: closed Mondays. Free on the third Thursday of each month for all visitors and daily for students and children. Foreign tourists pay more than Russian and Belarusian citizens. It drew 2,812,913 visitors in 2022 (Wikipedia).

Canada added Piotrovsky to its sanctions list in August 2023, and the Council of the European Union listed him on 23 April 2026, saying he "actively supported and justified Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine" (The Art Newspaper, 31 August 2023 and 29 April 2026).

In June 2022 Piotrovsky told Rossiiskaya Gazeta "We are all militarists and imperials" and "it is my country and I must be with it". On 2 October 2022 Dmitry Ozerkov, head of contemporary art, announced his resignation, saying "I don't intend to have anything in common with today's Russia" (USA Art News, 3 October 2022).

Unverified: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence (HUR) says the State Hermitage's Myrmekion expedition in occupied Crimea took 14 artifacts, and Ukrainian prosecutors notified the expedition's archaeologist Alexander Butyagin of suspicion in 2024 and changed the charge in 2026 to violations of the laws and customs of war (United24 Media, 7 October 2026).
details.funding_verdict: The State Hermitage Museum: mainly public: the Russian federal budget, with Gazprom as general sponsor of its Peter the Great Gallery
funding: The 1996 decree ordered the Government to fund the Hermitage's current maintenance from federal budget appropriations and to list its maintenance as a separate line in the federal budget from 1997 (Decree No. 862).

Gazprom was general sponsor of the permanent exhibition "Peter the Great Gallery", which opened in the Winter Palace on 14 January 2022; the chairman of Gazprom's management board, Alexey Miller, attended the opening, and Gazprom helped restore the ivory chandelier (Komsomolskaya Pravda, 17 January 2022). Two more halls opened on 21 June 2022 with Gazprom's support, and Piotrovsky thanked the company (AK&M, reprinting a Gazprom press release, 21 June 2022).

red_flags.heading: Fossil fuels
points: Gazprom was general sponsor of the Peter the Great Gallery opened in January 2022 and supported two further halls in June 2022 (Komsomolskaya Pravda, 17 January 2022; AK&M, 21 June 2022).

red_flags.heading: Boycott by partners and advisory bodies
points: After the 2022 invasion Hermitage Amsterdam returned a loan show and cut ties with the St Petersburg museum, the Hermitage Foundation UK cut ties, the International Advisory Board announced an "indefinite suspension" on 15 March 2022, and the Bizot group suspended Piotrovsky's membership (The Art Newspaper, 4 April 2022).

press.overall: The three pieces below, from 2022 to 2025, concern the director's stance on the war.

items.title: Sophia Kishkovsky, "Isolated by Russia boycotts, Hermitage director calls for 'cultural bridges between the nations'" (2022)
points: Piotrovsky had not condemned the invasion; he said "Putin's been my person since the 1990s" in a 2021 interview with the paper, and Putin awarded him Russia's Order of Friendship in 2016.

items.title: Romario, "State Hermitage Museum curator quits over Russia's war in Ukraine" (2022)
points: Reports Ozerkov's resignation and Piotrovsky's Rossiiskaya Gazeta interview backing the war.

items.title: Anna Matveeva, "The emperor" (2025)
points: Traces Piotrovsky from reformer to supporter of the war, says he publicly backed Putin in the 2012, 2018 and 2024 elections, and reports staff departures and a 2021 Proekt report that businesses tied to the Hermitage belonged to friends of his family.

details.bottom_line: The money behind the Hermitage is mainly the Russian state, which owns the museum and placed it under presidential patronage in 1996, with Gazprom as general sponsor of its Peter the Great Gallery in 2022. Canada (2023) and the EU (2026) sanctioned the director for his public support of the war, and European partners cut ties in 2022.

name: Victoria Gallery
watch: Sister institution of V-A-C ('Victoria, the Art of being Contemporary'). Second site Victoria Underground since 2020.
why_flagged: Sister institution of V-A-C ('Victoria, the Art of being Contemporary'). Second site Victoria Underground since 2020.
records_note: Its About page names founder Leonid Mikhelson and three managers.

overview: Private contemporary art gallery on the Volga embankment in the historic centre of Samara (gallery website).
Founded in 2005 by Leonid Mikhelson, a businessman from Novokuybyshevsk. The first director was Lyudmila Patrati (VK long read, Vse v Samare).
Named for Mikhelson's daughter Victoria, a name shared with the V-A-C Foundation (Kommersant FM).
The building closed for reconstruction in spring 2023. Since the reopening on 6 March 2026 the gallery occupies the whole three-storey building. Before it held one third (Snob, Kommersant FM).
On site: three exhibition halls, a lecture hall, a library, a bookshop, a cafe, studios, workshops and a roof exhibition space (VK long read).
Visiting: exhibition halls open Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 21:00. The site lists tours for blind and visually impaired visitors and with Russian Sign Language interpretation.
details.funding_verdict: Victoria Gallery: owner-funded: Leonid Mikhelson, whose wealth is in gas
funding: The gallery is private, founded and owned by Mikhelson (gallery website, Kommersant FM). Kommersant FM calls him the third-richest person on the Russian Forbes list.
Mikhelson is chairman of the management board of Novatek (UK Sanctions List), described as Russia's second-largest gas company (The Art Newspaper, 2022).

red_flags.heading: Owner's gas wealth and sanctions
points: Fossil fuels: the owner's fortune comes from Novatek, a gas company (The Art Newspaper; Coda Story).

UK: the UK Sanctions List (checked 24 October 2026) shows Mikhelson designated on 6 April 2022 with an asset freeze and travel ban, trust services sanctions from 21 March 2023 and a director disqualification from 9 April 2025. The ground is his directorships and shareholdings in Novatek and Sibur, in the energy and chemicals sectors.
New Zealand: the Russia Sanctions Register of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade lists him as sanctioned on 12 October 2022.
Ukraine: m24.ru reported on 20 October 2022 that President Zelensky enacted a National Security and Defence Council decision naming him.
Australia: Ukraine's Defence Intelligence sanctions page gives 6 April 2022.
Coda Story reports that the US sanctioned Novatek over Russia's annexation of Crimea.

Unverified: the Anti-Corruption Foundation (advocacy) says he controls companies that give financial and organisational help to the Russian Ministry of Defence, and the Dossier Center (investigative) lists him as suspected of giving a bribe, both as quoted by OpenSanctions.

press.overall: Pieces criticise Mikhelson and V-A-C, without naming the gallery.

items.title: Gareth Harris and José da Silva, "Venice gets political" (2022)
points: Global Project occupied V-A-C's Palazzo Zattere in Venice in May 2022 with banners reading "Let's expropriate Russian oligarchs for peace and climate justice", and criticised the EU for not sanctioning Mikhelson.
Does not name the Samara gallery.

items.title: "Putin's Oligarchs" series profile of Mikhelson (undated; events to March 2022)
points: Says Tate Modern, the Art Institute of Chicago and the New Museum kept accepting his money, and he served on their boards.
Notes that V-A-C's 26 February 2022 statement, "cannot turn a blind eye", stopped short of condemning the war.

wider_context: After the February 2022 invasion V-A-C left Instagram on 1 March 2022 and its artistic director Francesco Manacorda resigned in March 2022 (Coda Story). V-A-C's Venice palace was occupied by protesters in May 2022 and its activities suspended (The Art Newspaper, 19 May 2022).
The Samara gallery is Mikhelson's earlier project and is linked by name and by staff to V-A-C (VK long read, Kommersant FM); campaigners targeted V-A-C in Venice, not Samara.
The gallery's own news page says an exhibition, "Полный Сюр", closed early on 24 July 2026 because it could not meet fire safety requirements (stated by the space).
details.bottom_line: The money is one person's: Mikhelson, chairman of Novatek's management board, who is on the UK and New Zealand sanctions lists and, per Ukrainian sources, Ukraine's and Australia's. The gallery posts no accounts, board or partner list, so nothing beyond his ownership can be confirmed. Worth watching: how the gallery treats the war and sanctions in its programme, and the early-closed July 2026 show.

name: AlUla Arts & Cultural Oasis
funding: 100% state-funded by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia via the Royal Commission for AlUla (RCU), chaired directly by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MBS).
tier_note: No reason for the flag is recorded.

overview: The arts and culture programme of AlUla, an oasis region in north-western Saudi Arabia that spans roughly 22,561 square kilometres (Royal Commission for AlUla). The name "AlUla Arts & Cultural Oasis" does not appear on the visitor site.

Run by the Royal Commission for AlUla (RCU), founded in July 2017 and chaired since then by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (RCU website). Arab News (28 April 2021) says the Saudi Ministry of Finance set it up.

Venues and projects: Maraya, a 45-minute guided tour from SAR 95 per person. The Desert X AlUla biennial, launched in 2020. Wadi AlFann, a planned 65 square kilometre land-art site where Ahmed Mater is building installations (Al-Monitor). And the AlUla Arts Festival with the Centre Pompidou (Finestre sull'Arte).
Visiting: the visitor site gives a price only for the Maraya tour.
details.funding_verdict: AlUla Arts & Cultural Oasis: state-funded: the Saudi government through the Royal Commission for AlUla
funding: Arab News (28 April 2021): Saudi Arabia put in $2 billion of seed funding for AlUla's development; $3.2 billion for priority infrastructure was expected through public-private partnerships; the $15 billion masterplan runs in three phases to 2035.
Desert X AlUla was organised in collaboration with the RCU (The Art Newspaper, 17 January 2020; Hyperallergic, 8 October 2019).

red_flags.heading: Gulf state body
points: The RCU describes itself as a government body, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman since 2017 (RCU website).

red_flags.heading: Protest against Desert X AlUla
points: October 2019: three of Desert X's 14 board members, Ed Ruscha, Yael Lipschutz and Tristan Milanovich, resigned over Desert X's collaboration with the RCU. Hyperallergic (Hakim Bishara, 8 October 2019) says all three cited Saudi Arabia's human rights abuses and the killing of the journalist Jamal Khashoggi; Lipschutz wrote that Desert X "no longer reflected my values, my humanitarian values".

17 October 2019: Hyperallergic reports that the MaddocksBrown Foundation, a Los Angeles-based early donor that had given about $13,000 since 2017, pulled out. The headline ties the withdrawal to the Saudi collaboration.

press.overall: The criticism targets the Saudi state patronage behind AlUla's art, not individual works. Most dates from 2019.

items.title: Hakim Bishara, "Three Desert X Board Members Resign in Protest of Saudi Collaboration" (2019)
points: Reports the resignations and the reasons given. Lipschutz called the collaboration with the Saudi government "completely unethical". The RCU had not responded to the request for comment when the article ran (8 October 2019).

items.title: no author credited ("News Update"), "Desert X Funder Pulls Out in Protest of Saudi Collaboration" (2019)
points: Reports the MaddocksBrown Foundation withdrawal of about $13,000. Desert X's founder Susan Davis answered that "it is better to engage than to isolate".

items.title: Gareth Harris, "Desert X AlUla, the inaugural art biennial in a historic Saudi Arabian valley, announces participants" (2020)
points: Says the initiative "was met with a barrage of criticism" when announced in 2019. Quotes Lipschutz on "a deal with a national government… that is completely undemocratic" and Christopher Knight of the Los Angeles Times calling the move "morally corrupt".

items.title: Robbie Corey-Boulet, "Saudi artists marvel at surprise patron: their own rulers" (2022, drawing on AFP)
points: Critics of the Saudi royal family call the projects "artwashing", citing Khashoggi's killing and the poet Ashraf Fayadh, sentenced to death for apostasy in 2015 and later to eight years.
Mater welcomes state backing; AlDowayan says she has never been censored.

wider_context: Critics of the Saudi royal family call state-backed art projects "artwashing" for a country that silences dissidents (Al-Monitor, 2022).
The RCU, which the Crown Prince chairs, oversees AlUla, so its arts programme sits inside that critique.
details.bottom_line: The money behind AlUla's art is Saudi government money, channelled through a commission chaired by the Crown Prince. The weak point is the state patronage, which drew three board resignations and a donor withdrawal at Desert X AlUla in 2019. Worth watching: who the private partners in the public-private partnerships Arab News reported in 2021 are.

name: Musée Boribana
funding: Founded with private money by Boubacar Koné and actress CCH Pounder; Koné gave it to the Senegalese state in December 2014.
watch: Ngor museum of contemporary African art with artist studios and a residency. A conservator from the Ministry of Culture took office in March 2015.
records_note: The ministry page on Boribana gives its history and 2014 state handover but no budget, reports, accounts, funders or board.
affiliations_note: It has been a state museum since the founder donated it in December 2014 and sits with the Dak'Art Biennale and other state sites under the culture ministry.

overview: Museum of contemporary African art in Dakar, at the Rond-point Place ONU, Boulevard Dial Diop, corner Boulevard du Canal 4 (Senegalese culture ministry page).

Founded by the Senegalese anthropologist Boubacar Koné and his wife, the actress CCH Pounder (DakArtNews, 6 July 2026). Sources give different founding years: 1990 (culture ministry), 1992 (DakArtNews) and 1998 (Enquête+, 2015).
"Boribana" is Mandingo for "the race is over" (culture ministry page).

Designed as a grand piano, with four exhibition rooms on two levels, artists' studios for residencies, storage and a documentation room (culture ministry page). Enquête+ gives the land title as 1,000 m². DakArtNews adds a library and an outdoor cinema among later additions.
It opened with 34 works (DakArtNews, 6 July 2026). Enquête+ reports at least 400 artworks by artists of several nationalities in 2015.
The collection holds sculpture, ceramics, paintings, tapestries, photographs and video (culture ministry page).

Since 12 December 2014 it belongs to the Senegalese state. Enquête+ (25 March 2015) reports that Koné gave the museum to the state and also left the state the museum's land and artistic holdings. The same article announced that a conservator, Hawa Mara Ba, formerly a cultural adviser at the Ministry of Culture and Communication, would take up her post that week.
details.funding_verdict: Musée Boribana: founders' private money until the December 2014 gift to the Senegalese state
funding: Private origin: French Wikipedia states it was founded with private funds. DakArtNews (Remy Mallet, "She Helped Build Senegal's First Private Museum of Contemporary Art. Today, CCH Pounder Collects 'for the Future'", 6 July 2026) says Koné wanted Dakar to see the museum was built by Senegalese people, with the phrase "we had built it ourselves", and says the couple could not afford the provenance research and authentication that older African works require, so they collected contemporary art.

State since December 2014: Koné donated the museum to the Senegalese state on 12 December 2014; the culture ministry page says national authorities, including President Macky Sall, highly praised the gift.
details.bottom_line: The money behind the museum was the founders' own, from Koné and Pounder, until they gave it to the Senegalese state in December 2014; it now belongs to the state.

name: Musée des Civilisations Noires
funding: China financed the building with an RMB 180 million grant signed in 2010. The museum's own revenue was CFA 353.9 million in 2025.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Its site did not open from here.
highlight: A museum in Dakar built with a Chinese government grant and opened to the public on 6 December 2018.

overview: National museum in Dakar-Plateau, covering about 14,000 square metres, with a design inspired by the round huts of Casamance and room for 18,000 pieces (AFP via RTBF, 7 December 2018). Wikipedia places it in Dakar-Plateau.

Realises a vision of Senegal's first president Léopold Sédar Senghor for a museum on the histories and cultures of Black people (Wikipedia). Abdoulaye Wade laid the first stone. President Macky Sall inaugurated it on 6 December 2018, seven years later (AFP via RTBF; Mail & Guardian).

Building: a Chinese contractor built it (Mail & Guardian). The original design came from the Mexican architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, contracted in the 1970s under Senghor, with UNESCO covering his fee. Curator Ery Camara sees a Chinese pagoda in the circular form while others see Wolof houses (Mail & Guardian).

Opening exhibits (2018): the Toumaï skull, which came "exceptionally" from Chad, stone tools, megaliths more than 1,700 years old, Egyptian hieroglyphs, ritual masks and contemporary works including Abdoulaye Konaté's "Non au jihad à Tombouctou" (AFP via RTBF). The Mail & Guardian also reports Chinese masks among the inaugural exhibitions.

Director: Hamady Bocoum at the 2018 opening (Wikipedia). Professor Mouhamed Abdalah Ly was the museum's director in 2025 (Sud Quotidien via AllAfrica, 14 February 2026) and announced his resignation as Director General on his Facebook page in May 2026 (Sud Quotidien via AllAfrica, 26 May 2026).

2025: 49,308 entries between 1 January and 31 December, of which 19,408 were school audiences. Missions from China and Egypt chose the museum to celebrate their national days (Sud Quotidien via AllAfrica, Lamine Diedhiou, 14 February 2026).
details.funding_verdict: Musée des Civilisations Noires: Senegalese national museum, building paid by China
funding: China financed the museum with more than 30 million euros (AFP via RTBF, 2018). The Mail & Guardian puts the figure at about $34 million, paid largely by Beijing.
Own revenue reached 353.9 million FCFA in 2025, up 148% from 2024, from visits, rental of spaces and newly introduced merchandise (Sud Quotidien via AllAfrica, 14 February 2026).

press.overall: One critical report, written at the 2018 opening; later coverage is of results and management.

items.title: Sean O Toole, "Senegalese artistic heritage gets a home" (20 December 2018)
points: Calls the museum principally a symbol and, in the piece's words, most vulnerable as a symbol. Camara says a museum needs investment in "soft infrastructure: people, training, networks, alliances and, most importantly, vision".

Ery Camara says the seaside location makes climate control imperative and that Senegal has no professional conservators, so restoration work goes to Paris; he predicts a decline into obsolescence after the opening rush.
Chika Okeke-Agulu links the project to "cultural recolonisation" and warns that new money can create "monstrosities and white elephants".

Reports that the museum will not have any permanent displays, that its galleries were still empty two months before the opening, and that safety signs are in Chinese and English rather than Wolof or French.

details.bottom_line: The building was financed by China and the museum is a Senegalese national museum. Its own revenue was 353.9 million FCFA in 2025. Before the opening it was criticised for the Chinese-paid building, conservation capacity and empty galleries.

name: Center for Cultural Decontamination (CZKD)
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Independent non-profit cultural centre in the Veljković Pavilion at Birčaninova 21, Belgrade, known as "Kod Borke" after its founder (Radio Slobodna Evropa, 2010).
Founded by Borka Pavićević, formerly a principal of the Yugoslav Drama Theatre, in 1994 (Wikipedia). It began work at noon on 1 January 1995 with the "First Decontamination" (Vreme, 2025).

Established, in Wikipedia's words, as a response to the political and cultural climate in Serbia, working against nationalism, xenophobia, intolerance, hatred and fear. Vreme calls it the oldest anti-war centre in Serbia.
The pavilion was built in 1931 as Belgrade's first private museum (Sigrid Rausing Trust). Wikipedia says it was the courtyard art pavilion of the Veljković family house until 1941.

On site: a flexible theatre, a library, a smaller room for talks and book launches and a courtyard (Sigrid Rausing Trust). Programme categories on the website include film, exhibitions, concerts, theatre, performances, lectures, workshops, discussions, fairs, seminars and publishing, with long-running cycles such as CZKD Bioskop, FORA, Sokak and Svedočenja.

Pavićević said the centre hosted between four and five thousand programmes in its first 15 years. Shkelzen Maliqi recalled that a June 1997 exhibition of Albanian artists from Kosovo drew negative reactions from regime media in Belgrade and in Kosovo (Radio Slobodna Evropa, Branka Mihajlović, 10 February 2010).
In 2024, with the Polish Institute in Belgrade, it set up the "Borka Pavićević" award for public gesture, started on the initiative of Pavićević's admirers and friends in Poland (021.rs, 2026).
Visiting: office hours Monday to Friday, 11:00 to 18:00. Events are listed individually on the website.
details.funding_verdict: CZKD: grant-funded: foreign foundations, notably the Mott Foundation and the Sigrid Rausing Trust
funding: Mott Foundation: US$60,000 for 1 July 2013 to 30 June 2015 and a further US$60,000 for 1 July 2015 to 30 June 2017, both from its Civil Society programme for institutional and programmatic development (Mott Foundation grant records).
Sigrid Rausing Trust: lists CZKD as a grantee, supported from 2020 to 2024, with a total of £280,000 in previous grants (Sigrid Rausing Trust grantee profile).

press.overall: One criticism of the centre's foreign funding is recorded, by a film critic on television, and is known only from Wikipedia.

items.title: Ranko Munitić (2005), as recorded by Wikipedia
points: Unverified: Wikipedia, the only source, states that on 30 October 2005 the film critic Munitić criticised the centre's foreign funding on the B92 programme, arguing that the issue was reporting on their community abroad for large sums of money.

details.bottom_line: The money documented behind CZKD is grants from the Mott Foundation (2013 to 2017, US$120,000 in two grants) and the Sigrid Rausing Trust (supported 2020 to 2024, £280,000 in previous grants in total).

name: Tanoto Art Foundation
watch: RGE (pulp, palm oil) includes Pacific Oil & Gas (unverified claim).
why_flagged: RGE (pulp, palm oil) includes Pacific Oil & Gas (unverified claim).
records_note: Its About page names only a curator, a communications manager and an adviser.

overview: Private, not-for-profit art foundation in Singapore for contemporary art, "one of Singapore's first private art foundations" (stated by the foundation). Its address is UOB Plaza 1, 80 Raffles Place (e-flux directory).
Launched in January 2025 with a symposium, "Soul Song of a New Organisation", on 14 January 2025 at the School of the Arts, Singapore, during Singapore Art Week (e-flux).
Belinda Tanoto and Anderson Tanoto are the trustees. Xiaoyu Weng is artistic director (e-flux). ART SG says Belinda Tanoto, daughter of the Indonesian tycoon Sukanto Tanoto, founded it.
ART SG reports it plans a permanent space.
Programme: talks in Sao Paulo and Hong Kong, and support for commissions at the Singapore Biennale 2025 (ART SG).

First exhibition: "Rituals of Perception", 21 January to 1 March 2026 at New Bahru School Hall, curated by Weng, with more than twenty artists. Several works come from the Tanoto Family Collection. Weekly public programmes are free (e-flux).
details.funding_verdict: Tanoto Art Foundation: family-funded by the Tanoto family; the foundation publishes no funders or accounts
funding: The trustees are children of Sukanto Tanoto, whose Royal Golden Eagle group (RGE) has businesses in paper, palm oil, viscose, construction, energy, property and asset management (Wikipedia). RGE's energy arm Pacific Energy, formerly Pacific Oil & Gas, explores for gas in Canada and runs an LNG terminal and a gas power plant in China (Wikipedia).
Works in its first exhibition come from the Tanoto Family Collection (e-flux).

press.overall: Coverage found is launch and exhibition announcements and one profile on ART SG's own site.

wider_context: Greenpeace's 2013 report called Sukanto Tanoto's business empire "the single largest driver of deforestation in the world identified by Greenpeace"; APRIL denies the claims and pledged in June 2015 to end deforestation in its supply chain (Wikipedia).

30 October 2024: ICIJ and The Gecko Project reported that seven of nine former employees said the Tanoto family controlled Borneo Hijau Lestari, a pulpwood group linked to major deforestation. Unverified: the ownership claim, from former employees and Greenpeace; RGE calls it "unfounded, unsupported and untrue" (ICIJ).

8 February 2021: OCCRP reported that Tanoto bought the Ludwig complex in Munich in July 2019 for about 348 million euros through Luxembourg and offshore companies; Indonesia's financial intelligence head said his agency was investigating tax issues involving Tanoto's companies (OCCRP).
None of these pieces names the foundation; the connection is that the foundation's trustees are the family's children.
details.bottom_line: The foundation does not say where its money comes from, and the only link read is the family that owns RGE, which includes a gas business and pulp and palm oil companies facing deforestation allegations. Worth watching: any donor list or accounts, and the planned permanent space.

name: Kapelica Gallery (Kersnikova Institute)
funding: Small NGO venue (2025), funded by Slovenia's Ministry of Culture, the City of Ljubljana and EU programmes.
watch: Research-art gallery founded in 1995 by the University of Ljubljana's Student Organisation (ŠOU). Run by Kersnikova with the BioTehna lab and Rampa hacker space.
records_note: Its Crew page names a director and staff.
affiliations_note: Run by the Kersnikova Institute, founded by the University of Ljubljana's student organisation; a member of EMAP with LABoral, iMAL, Ars Electronica and Onassis. Member of European Media Art Platform.

overview: Contemporary and research-based art gallery in Ljubljana, listed by the Slovenian culture portal at Likozarjeva ulica 1, where the Kersnikova Institute moved in 2021.

Established in 1995 by the Student Organisation of the University of Ljubljana (ŠOU), according to the Slovenian culture portal culture.gov.si. Jurij Krpan, an architect and curator, has led the gallery since its founding (culture.gov.si).
Named for a former chapel (kapelica) at Kersnikova 4, the gallery's earlier premises (culture.gov.si).

Managed by the Kersnikova Institute, a Ljubljana nonprofit founded in 2000 as the K6/4 Institute through a restructuring of the University of Ljubljana's Student Organisation, which remains a founder. It took the name Kersnikova in 2014 (culture.gov.si).

Programme: spatial installations, performances, sound research and lectures on scientific and technological applications, biopolitics and urban phenomena (Kersnikova). Artists shown have included Stelarc, Orlan and Survival Research Laboratories (culture.gov.si).
Kersnikova also runs BioTehna, a laboratory for artistic research into living systems founded in 2012, and Rampa, a hacker laboratory and incubator for young creators founded in 2013 (Kersnikova).
details.funding_verdict: Kapelica Gallery (Kersnikova Institute): supported by the Slovenian Ministry of Culture, the City of Ljubljana and European Union programmes
funding: Kersnikova's website lists 21 supporters under its supporter entries: the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Slovenia and the City of Ljubljana (Mestna občina Ljubljana); ŠOU; the European Commission, Creative Europe, Horizon 2020, the European Regional Development Fund, Interreg DIVA and the Swiss contribution; and the projects ART4MED, Arc-hive, STARTS, CreaTures, Biofriction, MAST, SYSTEM, DOIT, DITOS, AILab, konS and MJU.
The Slovenian culture portal lists EU-funded Kersnikova projects from 2003 to 2025, including Creative Europe projects.
details.bottom_line: The Slovenian Ministry of Culture and the City of Ljubljana are named as supporters of the Kersnikova Institute, which manages the gallery, alongside European Union programmes and ŠOU, the student organisation that founded it.

name: Origins Centre
funding: Wits campus museum, opened 2006; its Rock Art Research Institute is funded by the National Research Foundation, Wits' research fund and Anglo American's Chairman's Fund.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: Parent Wits University posts annual reports 2006 to 2025 with audited accounts and lists its Council.
affiliations_note: A museum on the West campus of the University of the Witwatersrand, showing rock art from Wits's Rock Art Research Institute. Wits Art Museum belongs to the same university.

overview: Museum of human origins of the University of the Witwatersrand (Wits) at Yale Road and Enoch Sontonga Avenue on Wits' West campus, Braamfontein, Johannesburg, on a site above the M1 highway across from Braamfontein cemetery (Wits; Mail & Guardian, 13 April 2006).
Opened by President Thabo Mbeki in 2006 (Wits; South African History Online). South African History Online lists it as part of the Wits Faculty of Science.
Built on the site of the fine art department's studios, known as "The Wedge" (Mail & Guardian, 13 April 2006).
Designed by Craig McClenaghan of Mashabane Rose and Associates. The Mail & Guardian says he designed the halls to feel like caves, with dark spaces and walls "a metre thick".

On show: hominin innovation from over 2 million years ago, stone tools, San beliefs, the impact of colonialism and examples of resistance, and a rock art collection from Wits' Rock Art Research Institute (RARI) (Wits). Artworks include Walter Oltman's woven map of the Earth and Willem Boshoff's "Signs of People" (Mail & Guardian).

Open Monday to Friday 09:00 to 17:00 and Saturday and public holidays 09:00 to 16:00. Closed Sunday. Tickets are booked online through Webtickets, and guided tours are booked in advance. The visitor car park is access controlled: call the centre for the code and bring ID (Wits).
details.funding_verdict: Origins Centre: university museum: part of the Wits Faculty of Science
funding: South African History Online lists the centre as part of the Wits Faculty of Science; it is presented on the Wits website, which links to a Wits giving page for donations (South African History Online; Wits).
Its rock art collection comes from the Rock Art Research Institute (RARI) at Wits (Wits).
details.bottom_line: The Origins Centre is part of the Wits Faculty of Science, so the university is its institutional home, and the centre takes donations through the Wits giving page.

name: Amorepacific Museum of Art
funding: Corporate museum run directly by Amorepacific Corp (site footer, 2026); cosmetics money. Current LeWitt show co-organised with MOT Tokyo.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The museum posts nothing itself; its parent Amorepacific posts audit reports 2015 to 2024, sustainability reports 2017 to 2025 and its board.

overview: Corporate art museum inside the Amorepacific global headquarters at Hangang-daero 100, Yongsan-gu, Seoul (museum site; W Magazine, Ann Binlot, 27 August 2025).
The headquarters opened in Yongsan in 2018 (Wikipedia). W Magazine places the museum in David Chipperfield's "luminous cube". Directed by Seungchang Jeon (press release, December 2025).
The museum shows ancient Korean art and contemporary art. It also supports researchers and young writers (Artessere).
The building holds exhibition space in the basement and an atrium over the first three floors with the lobby, shop, the "APMA Cabinet" exhibition space and apLAP, a library (Artessere).

2026 programme: "APMA, Chapter Five", 1 April to 2 August, about 50 works by over 40 artists from the museum's contemporary collection. "Jonas Wood", 1 September 2026 to 28 February 2027. And "Sol LeWitt: Open Structure" in the second half of 2026, planned by the museum in collaboration with the Sol LeWitt Foundation and the Tokyo Metropolitan Museum of Contemporary Art (exhibition page). The first two dates are from the press release of 23 December 2025.
Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 6 pm. Closed Mondays, 1 January and the Seollal and Chuseok holidays. W Magazine (27 August 2025) described admission as free.
details.funding_verdict: Amorepacific Museum of Art: corporate-owned: hosted in the headquarters of Amorepacific Corp
funding: The museum's website is run by Amorepacific Corp. and the museum sits in the company's headquarters (museum site; W Magazine).

Amorepacific was founded in 1945 by Sungwhan Suh as Pacific Chemical; he handed it to his second son Kyungbae Suh in 1997. The parent is Amorepacific Holdings (renamed from Amorepacific Group in 2025). 2025 revenue was 4.25 trillion won and net income 247.3 billion won (Wikipedia).
wider_context: The Korea Fair Trade Commission fined Amorepacific 500 million won in August 2014 for forcing door-to-door sales agencies to send high-performing employees to new or struggling agencies. The commission said it was the highest fine it could impose because it could not obtain documentation for door-to-door sales (Korea JoongAng Daily, 18 August 2014).

On 6 April 2020 the commission fined Amorepacific Group and its affiliate Cosvision 48 million won each, 96 million won in total, over fixed deposits of 75 billion won given to Cosvision without a fee, which helped it obtain five low-interest loans from the Korea Development Bank worth 60 billion won (Korea Times, 6 April 2020; the article body also prints 9.6 billion won, inconsistent with its headline).
Both cases concern the museum's owner, Amorepacific.
details.bottom_line: The museum is a company museum: Amorepacific, a cosmetics group, hosts it in its headquarters. The company's weak points are a 2014 fine of 500 million won and a 2020 fine of 48 million won from the Korea Fair Trade Commission.
